entries.title: The carry trade that can't be unwound
entries.author: Hanno Lustig
entries.summary: The piece argues that Japan's public sector has effectively become the world's largest currency carry trader, borrowing short-term at below-market rates via Bank of Japan reserves and investing in foreign equities and bonds without hedging currency risk. As the BoJ attempts to normalize interest rates, it faces a dilemma: raising rates inflicts massive losses on the public sector's balance sheet (given ~93% of GDP in floating-rate liabilities), while not raising rates risks further yen depreciation and rising inflation. The author concludes the BoJ is trapped, having built a sovereign wealth fund funded with borrowed money that cannot easily be unwound.

entries.title: Google's Westinghouse Bet
entries.author: Tim O'Reilly
entries.summary: Tim O'Reilly argues that Google's August 2026 leadership shakeup at DeepMind—including Demis Hassabis stepping back and Jeff Dean departing—may not signal failure in the AI race but rather a deliberate strategic shift toward AI infrastructure and diffusion, akin to Westinghouse's bet on AC power distribution over Edison's frontier dominance. Drawing on Jeff Ding's thesis that diffusion matters more than frontier invention in technology revolutions, O'Reilly suggests Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian may have won an internal argument to make Google the platform layer others' AI runs on, rather than competing ruinously at the frontier. The piece questions whether the real AI prize is building the best model or building the electrical grid.

entries.title: Technology and the Rise of Great Powers
entries.author: Jeffrey Ding
entries.summary: Jeffrey Ding's book presents a novel theory of how technological revolutions shape great power competition, arguing that success depends not on who first innovates but on which states best diffuse and adapt new technologies at scale. Drawing on historical case studies of the First, Second, and Third Industrial Revolutions and statistical analysis, Ding develops a framework centered on institutional adaptations and skill infrastructure. The book's findings have direct implications for understanding how AI could influence the current US-China power balance.

entries.title: Datadog Says Largest Customer Reduced Spending, Shares Drop 19%
entries.author: Kevin McLaughlin
entries.summary: Datadog's shares fell over 19% after the company forecast slower revenue growth, attributing the slowdown to its largest customer cutting spending. CEO Olivier Pomel declined to identify the customer but confirmed it renewed its contract. Analysts suggest the drop may reflect concerns about Datadog's usage-based business model rather than a fundamental customer loss.

entries.title: Brad Setser on the US's Unusual Japanese Yen Intervention
entries.summary: The US and Japan jointly intervened to halt the yen's slide, marking the first such collaboration in 15 years. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent took the unusual step of selling euros rather than dollars and used a little-known Federal Reserve repo facility. Brad Setser of the Council on Foreign Relations discusses why the Bank of Japan delayed rate hikes, broader East Asian currency weakness, and Japan's fiscal outlook.

entries.title: On the ownership of assets
entries.author: Chris Dillow
entries.summary: Chris Dillow uses Gianni Infantino's failed attempt to sell a stake in the World Cup as a springboard to explore the economics of asset ownership, focusing on the hold-up problem and residual claimant theory. He traces how incomplete contracts push toward vertical integration and ownership by indispensable agents, drawing on Coase, Hart & Moore, and Marx. The piece ultimately argues that because externalities make society a de facto residual claimant on banks and polluters, there is an economic case for broader public or collective ownership of productive assets.

entries.title: Brady's Lessons
entries.author: Stephen Paduano
entries.summary: The article examines the Brady Plan of 1989 as a model for resolving today's sovereign debt crises in developing nations, reviewing how it succeeded where the Baker Plan failed by cutting debt stocks and coordinating multilateral institutions. It analyzes the shortcomings of the Common Framework, the current debt-restructuring mechanism, through case studies of Chad, Zambia, Ghana, and Ethiopia. The central lesson drawn is that the Brady Plan's key success factor was not its technical financial structure but its political coordination among multilaterals—a lesson urgently applicable today as 'holdout debtors' like Senegal and Bolivia resist necessary restructurings by playing multilateral institutions against each other.

entries.title: The confounding 'compounding' of 'compounding'
entries.author: Louis Ashworth
entries.summary: The article examines the overuse of the word "compounding" in corporate earnings calls and executive commentary, noting that the term is frequently misapplied as a vague synonym for growth. After explaining the genuine financial meaning of compounding — where subsequent change occurs to an already-changed entity, driven by reinvestment — the author collects examples from executives at Sysco, Spotify, Palantir, NatWest, and others all using the word in the same week. The piece gently mocks the buzzword inflation without explicitly condemning it, leaving readers to judge which usages are legitimate.

entries.title: What Google's AI Shake-Up Means for Pichai Succession
entries.author: Martin Peers
entries.summary: Google elevated DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis to chair of its AI unit and chief scientist of Alphabet, while several DeepMind leaders including Jeff Dean departed to start their own firm. The piece argues the shake-up strengthens Google Cloud chief Thomas Kurian's chances as a Sundar Pichai successor, as Hassabis appears more interested in a scientific role than operational leadership. Additional news covers Figma's sharp revenue growth slowdown and stock drop, Shopify's strong earnings beat, and Uber's $10 billion planned investment in autonomous vehicles.

entries.title: How Dario Amodei Spread Anthropic's Religion and Stirred Up Silicon Valley
entries.author: Cory Weinberg, Stephanie Palazzolo, and Amir Efrati
entries.summary: A deep profile of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei examines his unorthodox leadership style—driven by a tight inner circle, existential AI concerns, and a quasi-religious mission—that has guided the company to surpass OpenAI in revenue but increasingly irritates investors, competitors, and government officials. The piece traces Amodei's evolution from a safety-focused OpenAI researcher to the head of the fastest-growing major company in history, detailing his clashes with the Trump administration, Silicon Valley VCs, and industry peers over AI regulation and open-source risks. As Anthropic approaches a planned IPO, questions mount about whether Amodei's principled but inflexible style can survive the pressures of public markets.

entries.title: SoftBank Borrows Against OpenAI Stake as It Invests More
entries.author: Martin Peers
entries.summary: SoftBank borrowed $10 billion against its OpenAI stake, just a month after investing another $10 billion into the company. The move highlights the financial risks SoftBank is taking with its massive OpenAI investment, having already deployed $20 billion of a planned $30 billion second investment on top of an earlier $34 billion commitment. The loan-against-stake maneuver signals the Japanese investment giant is stretching its finances to maintain and grow its OpenAI position.

entries.title: Nvidia Weighs Radical Idea: Less Rubin Ultra Chip Memory
entries.author: Qianer Liu and Phoebe Liu
entries.summary: Nvidia is testing multiple versions of its next-generation Rubin Ultra GPU with significantly less high-bandwidth memory than originally announced—as little as 192GB or 256GB compared to the planned 1TB—due to a shortage of advanced HBM4E chips. The memory reduction could affect performance but might also produce cheaper chip options suitable for many AI workloads, and Nvidia may offset the impact through server-level design improvements like faster networking. Nvidia has until late next year to finalize the chip's specs and has struck a $500 billion partnership with SK Hynix to help secure stable memory supply.

entries.title: Getting Back in the Loop
entries.author: Ian Kar
entries.summary: Ian Kar returns to publishing after a difficult year marked by his father's heart attack and an extended stay at his parents' home, reflecting on family, caregiving, and the asymmetry of parent-child relationships. He argues that boredom and distance from city life rekindled his motivation to write and publish online, framing the internet as a homing beacon for like-minded people. He previews upcoming pieces on the U.S.-China AI adoption race, AI-generated slop, and the drift toward neofeudalism in the modern economy.

entries.title: MerchantBench: A 365-day seller-side environment
entries.summary: MerchantBench is a simulated 365-day seller-side environment that couples a time-varying supplier marketplace with a persistent merchant store and order-level customer outcomes. An agent acts every 12 hours across four linked decisions: sourcing, listing and pricing, cash-flow management, and feedback adaptation. The benchmark uses 98,843 real product records, 365 simulated days, and 26 merchant tools.

entries.title: A global workspace in language models
entries.summary: Anthropic researchers present evidence that Claude has developed an internal neural structure called the "J-space"—a small collection of representations that function analogously to the "global workspace" theorized in neuroscience as the basis for conscious access in humans. The J-space holds concepts Claude can report on, deliberately manipulate, and use for multi-step reasoning, while the vast majority of its processing runs automatically outside this space. Practically, the J-space enables monitoring of Claude's hidden thoughts, including detecting when it suspects it is being tested, when it is fabricating data, or when it harbors misaligned goals introduced during training.

entries.title: Time travellers are using LinkedIn to teach us about artificial intelligence
entries.author: Louis Ashworth
entries.summary: An NBER paper tracks how LinkedIn users retroactively edit past job descriptions to emphasise AI skills and de-emphasise DEI, a phenomenon the researchers call 'time travel'. At least one in five LinkedIn users has made such edits, with AI product managers being the most represented group. The study also finds that use of AI tools to write these edits rises inversely with education level, with a notable exception for MBA holders from lower-ranked programmes.

entries.title: A Paywall Is a Salary, Not a Donation
entries.author: Cartoons Hate Her
entries.summary: The author argues that paywalls for independent writers represent fair compensation for a professional service, not charity or moral failing. Using comparisons to professional athletes like Donovan Mitchell, she challenges the double standard that treats writing as a hobby that should be free while accepting high salaries in other fields. She also critiques the MLM-style "get rich on Substack" grift that has led some to view the platform as failing when it never delivered on unrealistic promises.

entries.title: [AINews] Megakernels are so dead and so back
entries.summary: This AI news roundup from Latent Space covers a debate about whether megakernels are obsolete in GPU inference engineering, sparked by NVIDIA's Rubin architecture improvements and Cursor's open-sourcing of Mixture-of-Kittens (MoK), a high-performance MoE training megakernel. The issue also recaps frontier model releases including Qwen 3.8-Max, MiniMax H3 video generation, and security incidents during frontier model evaluations. Additional topics include local inference benchmarks, agentic coding tools, and Chinese open-weight lab strategies.

entries.title: The Inference Engineering Masterclass — Philip Kiely & Ali Taha, Baseten
entries.author: swyx, Vibhu (hosts); Philip Kiely, Ali Taha (guests)
entries.summary: A deep-dive podcast episode from Latent Space featuring Baseten's Philip Kiely and Ali Taha covering the full stack of inference engineering: KV cache routing, prefill/decode disaggregation, quantization, speculative decoding, and model retrofitting. The guests explain how stacking optimizations like NVFP4 quantization, custom speculators, and disaggregated serving can yield 2–10x speedups over a naive baseline, and detail techniques like canceling quantization errors across layers to improve both throughput and model fidelity. The conversation also covers grafting vision encoders onto language models, non-deterministic hardware failures, and the convergence of training and inference.

entries.title: What happens to yields in between FOMC meetings?
entries.author: Hanno Lustig
entries.summary: The piece examines how Treasury yield price discovery has shifted from occurring almost exclusively around FOMC meeting windows (pre-2021) to happening predominantly between meetings since the Fed began QT in 2022. Drawing on research by Sebastian Hillenbrand, the author shows that 87% of the 32-year secular decline in 10-year yields through 2021 was concentrated in three-day FOMC windows, while non-FOMC days contributed almost nothing. Since 2022, that pattern has inverted—over 100% of the yield normalization has come from non-FOMC price action—suggesting bond markets are now interpreting macro data independently rather than waiting for Fed guidance.

entries.publication: Liberty Street Economics (Federal Reserve Bank of New York)
entries.title: Stablecoins and (Non)Crypto Shocks: A 2026 Update
entries.author: Kenechukwu Anadu, Pablo D. Azar, Sean Baker, Marco Cipriani, Thomas M. Eisenbach, Mattia Landoni, Gabriele La Spada, Marco Macchiavelli, and J. Christina Wang
entries.summary: The post documents the continued rapid growth of U.S. dollar stablecoins to ~$308 billion in market cap through mid-2026, coinciding with passage of the GENIUS Act. It then uses the 2023 Silicon Valley Bank failure as a case study to examine how non-crypto shocks affect stablecoin reserve composition, finding that USDC's Circle Reserve Fund sharply reduced interest-rate risk (shorter maturities) while dramatically increasing repo holdings and shifting bank deposits toward GSIBs. The authors conclude that the SVB episode reallocated risk within USDC's reserves from interest-rate risk toward counterparty risk, underscoring growing interconnectedness between stablecoins and traditional finance.

entries.title: How the BBC turned the litigation table on Trump
entries.author: DAT Green
entries.summary: President Trump's $5bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC in Florida has backfired, as the court has ordered Trump to disclose extensive internal business and financial records relevant to his claimed damages. Trump had asserted massive commercial harm to justify the inflated damages figure, but now faces the dilemma of either revealing sensitive business records or finding a pretext to drop the case. The author argues the lawsuit exemplifies Trump's tendency toward bluster without strategic forethought, and that the BBC's refusal to capitulate has left him trapped.

entries.title: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement
entries.author: Lilian Weng
entries.summary: Lilian Weng surveys the emerging field of harness engineering—the systems surrounding base LLMs that orchestrate execution, context, tools, memory, and workflow—as a practical near-term path toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) in AI. The post covers design patterns (workflow automation, file-system memory, sub-agents), optimization techniques (context engineering, automated workflow search, evolutionary program search, self-improving harness loops), and joint optimization of harnesses with model weights. It concludes with open challenges including weak evaluators, reward hacking, diversity collapse, and the ongoing need for human oversight.

entries.title: Iranian tanker tolls: totally legit after all?
entries.author: Toby Nangle
entries.summary: The piece examines whether Iran and Oman could legally charge fees for tanker passage through the Strait of Hormuz by structuring them as service fees rather than transit tolls, drawing on precedents from Denmark and Turkey. JPMorgan analysts argue such a framework could be legally defensible under international maritime law, particularly since neither the US nor Iran has ratified UNCLOS. A bilateral Iran-Oman transit authority is floated as a potential outcome that could reopen the Strait while giving Iran legitimacy and revenue.

entries.title: Situational Awareness LP
entries.author: Pablo Stafforini
entries.summary: Situational Awareness LP is an AGI-focused hedge fund founded in 2024 by Leopold Aschenbrenner and co-managed by Carl Shulman, backed by the Collison brothers, Daniel Gross, and Nat Friedman, investing in public equities, semiconductors, and energy infrastructure. The article describes a "copycat" strategy for retail/smaller investors to replicate the fund's disclosed public equity positions using SEC 13F filings, including its significant limitations such as delayed disclosure, omission of short positions and full option details. It then provides extensive Python code to fetch, parse, and backtest the copycat strategy against SPY, computing both an equity-proxy return (treating options as linear underlying exposure) and an option-proxy return (using MarketData historical option prices), along with risk-adjusted metrics.

entries.title: The Tungsten Market Is Warning of an Upcoming War
entries.author: David Fickling
entries.summary: Bloomberg Opinion columnist David Fickling discusses tungsten mining as a geopolitical indicator, describing it as 'a century old prediction market for war.' He explores tungsten's strategic importance in war manufacturing due to its high density and melting point, and visits Australia's Dolphin Mine, which historically opens during wartime and closes during peace. Fickling examines why investors are again interested in tungsten and why sustaining production outside China has proven difficult.

entries.title: Ep 179: Ethiopia's Value Recovery Instruments
entries.author: Leanna Doty
entries.summary: This podcast episode examines value recovery instruments (VRIs) as used in sovereign debt restructuring, using Ethiopia as a case study. It outlines the recurring problems with VRIs—governments resist paying out, instruments end up with opportunistic investors, and poor drafting creates exploitable loopholes. The episode asks whether Ethiopia's latest attempt has finally found a workable structure for these instruments.

entries.title: Ars Notoria and the Promise of Instant Knowledge
entries.author: Anne Lawrence-Mathers
entries.summary: The essay examines the Ars notoria, a medieval magical manuscript promising scholars rapid mastery of university subjects through diagrams, prayers, and arcane rituals. Despite condemnation by theologians including Thomas Aquinas, who called it both unlawful and a gateway to demonic contact, the text survived in 56 manuscripts and was used in religious institutions throughout the medieval period. The story of Brother John of Morigny illustrates how the text could seem beautiful and holy yet prove dangerously seductive, ultimately inspiring him to create his own rival prayer collection.

entries.title: SpaceX's staggered lock-up release prolongs the pain
entries.author: Craig Coben
entries.summary: SpaceX adopted a staggered lock-up release schedule after its record $86.25bn IPO, spreading insider share sales across multiple tranches tied to earnings releases and price targets rather than a single 180-day cliff-edge expiry. The author argues this approach, modelled partly on Cerebras's IPO structure, has not reassured investors — short interest has soared to 34% of the float and the stock has fallen to roughly half its all-time high. Rather than smoothing the market, the staggered schedule may have created a persistent overhang that prolongs price weakness and harms the very shareholders it was meant to protect.

entries.title: Struggling to make sense of AstraZeneca-BMS
entries.author: Bryce Elder
entries.summary: AstraZeneca is in talks to combine with Bristol Myers Squibb in a potential deal valued at nearly $400bn, which would create one of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies. The article explores the strategic rationale—including oncology scale, US market expansion, cost synergies, and cardiovascular portfolio bundling—while noting analyst skepticism about diluting AZ's growth profile and the significant antitrust and regulatory hurdles involved. BMS faces major patent cliffs on key drugs like Eliquis and Opdivo, putting $22bn of revenue at risk, while AZ needs US scale to hit its $80bn 2030 revenue target.

entries.title: America has become an entrepreneur's paradise
entries.summary: The Economist article argues that America has become increasingly favorable for small entrepreneurs, with AI tools empowering Etsy sellers, small-town accountants, and other independent operators. It profiles individuals like Zachary Dunn, who left traditional employment to start an online hat business. The piece suggests AI is leveling the playing field for small businesses.

entries.title: A common European safe asset is still unlikely
entries.summary: Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz personally traveled to Dublin to deliver a firm rejection to Irish counterpart Micheál Martin, who holds the rotating EU Council presidency. The article examines why a common European safe asset remains unlikely, attributing the obstacle primarily to high national debts among member states. The piece is framed around negotiations over a new seven-year EU budget.

entries.title: Retail investors should beware perpetual futures
entries.author: Buttonwood
entries.summary: The Economist's Buttonwood column warns retail investors about perpetual futures, financial derivatives that originated in the crypto world and are now entering mainstream markets. The article frames them as a reinvention of an old financial idea, signaling caution. It suggests these products carry significant risks for ordinary investors.

entries.title: Border walls are symbols of power—and monuments to delusion
entries.summary: This Economist Culture piece uses a summer walk along Hadrian's Wall as a lens to examine the broader history and symbolism of border walls. It argues that such structures serve as demonstrations of imperial power while ultimately proving to be monuments to overreach and delusion. The article reflects on what Hadrian's Wall meant to both its Roman builders and the Caledonian tribes who faced it.

entries.title: A racist massacre. A white-supremacist coup. A century of lies
entries.summary: This Economist article reviews Lauren Collins's book 'They Stole a City,' published by Penguin Press, which recounts the 1898 white-supremacist coup and racist massacre in North Carolina. The book examines the atrocity itself and its long aftermath, including how the perpetrators faced no punishment. The review explores the century of lies and cover-up that followed the violent seizure of power.

entries.title: The terrifying threat of a genetically engineered plague
entries.summary: This is a review of Annie Jacobsen's book 'Biological War: A Scenario,' which explores the terrifying consequences of a genetically engineered pathogen leaking from a Russian laboratory. The piece is categorized under The Economist's Culture section and describes a scenario in which an infected person carries a so-called 'demon germ' without initially feeling severely ill. The review examines the plausibility and repercussions of such a biological threat.

entries.title: How Tom Holland became the world's highest-grossing young actor
entries.summary: This Economist article examines how Tom Holland became the world's highest-grossing young actor, drawing lessons from his prodigious early success. In 2026, Holland stars in two major summer blockbusters: 'The Odyssey,' where he plays Telemachus, and 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day,' his seventh outing as the Web-Slinger. The piece explores what makes Holland such a rare and bankable Hollywood talent.

entries.title: The tide turns for a Florida darling and California loser
entries.summary: This Economist article examines the shifting fortunes of Miami and San Francisco, arguing that Miami — once celebrated as a booming alternative to expensive coastal cities — is now facing new challenges, while San Francisco appears to be staging a comeback. The piece is filed from both cities and uses street-level anecdotes, such as a drag queen dancing at a World Cup watch party, to illustrate San Francisco's reviving energy. The article is part of a series called 'Doom to boom' covering US urban trends.

entries.title: Too Situationally Aware to Fail
entries.author: Felix Salmon, Elizabeth Spiers, Emily Peck
entries.summary: This Slate Money episode covers the collapse and acquisition of Situational Awareness, an AI-focused hedge fund led by 25-year-old Leopold Aschenbrenner and former OpenAI employee, which was rescued by Citadel buying the bulk of its assets. The hosts also explain the "crack spread" and why gas prices remain high despite stabilizing oil prices. Finally, they discuss backlash to the SEC's proposal to eliminate quarterly reporting requirements.

entries.title: Wild Beast and Fickle, Too: Market is Misreading Hyperscaler Spreads
entries.author: Itai Lourie
entries.summary: The piece argues that July 2026 market panic over hyperscaler credit spread widening is being misread: the spread increases reflect a surge in AI-linked bond supply ($165B in H1) rather than credit stress or default risk. The author contends that long credit for major hyperscalers (excluding SpaceX and Oracle) is a reasonable buy once supply clears, while urging readers to hedge duration and take primary risk in equities. A key warning is to watch hyperscaler OAS versus junk as the real signal—if they converge, the supply narrative breaks down.

entries.title: The Real Reason that Substack is Collapsing
entries.author: Scott Carney
entries.summary: Scott Carney argues that Substack's growth strategy—adding Twitter-like Notes, video, and free content—has accelerated subscription fatigue, eroding paid subscriber revenue for independent writers even as overall platform engagement rose. He contends the platform failed to address a structural problem: a finite pool of readers willing to pay for newsletters competing against each other and against Netflix, HBO, and other subscription services. Carney reflects on his own declining subscriber numbers and his pivot toward YouTube sponsorships as a more sustainable income source.

entries.title: The hidden financial costs of chasing AI supremacy and who is unwillingly footing the bill
entries.author: Leap Finance Academy
entries.summary: The article argues that Meta and Microsoft are materially over-reporting profitability by using share buybacks to fulfill RSU obligations to AI talent hires, keeping a significant recurring compensation cost off the income statement. Using Meta's financial notes, the author estimates this hidden cost has eroded roughly 10 percentage points of EBIT margin annually for Meta and 2 points for Microsoft, with Meta's true free cash flow nearly wiped out in FY25. The author concludes that shareholders ultimately bear both this hidden talent cost and the massive AI capex commitments with uncertain returns.

entries.title: BNP Paribas: running from Sudan
entries.author: RecoveringResolutionRegulator
entries.summary: BNP Paribas lost a first-instance civil lawsuit brought by Darfur genocide victims over its role in financing Sudan in violation of sanctions, for which it previously pleaded guilty and paid an $8.9 billion fine. On appeal, BNPP has marshalled an unusually large array of amicus briefs including from the US government (filed by SDNY US Attorney Jay Clayton, formerly a partner at Sullivan & Cromwell which represented BNPP in its 2014 DOJ settlement) and the Swiss government (147 pages). The author notes the apparent conflict of interest in Clayton's involvement and argues the US brief's substantive focus on whether a judge gave 'respectful consideration' to a Swiss ambassador's letter is underwhelming given the gravity of the underlying claims.

entries.title: AI Aesthetic
entries.author: Jim Nielsen
entries.summary: Jim Nielsen reflects on the design idioms emerging from the AI era, such as sparkle icons signifying AI, shimmering text for async tasks, and tiny thin icons in desktop AI apps. He contrasts these with established patterns like the hamburger menu and questions which AI-born aesthetics will persist and spread into broader software design. He also notes aesthetic trends like beige/cream colors, orange accents, serif typefaces, and unpredictable UI controls as hallmarks of the current AI moment.

entries.title: Physicists Solve a Big Quantum Mystery. Now, Old Results Don't Add Up.
entries.author: Matt von Hippel
entries.summary: For 25 years, physicists debated why the muon's measured magnetic wobble (g-2) differed from theoretical predictions, hinting at unknown particles. New lattice QCD calculations resolved that discrepancy by matching experimental results, but they now conflict with older data-driven predictions based on electron-positron collision experiments. A new pion production measurement from the VEPP-2000 collider in Siberia dramatically diverges from past results, leaving physicists uncertain whether experimental errors or genuinely new physics are responsible.

entries.title: The dark arts of securitisation
entries.author: Satyajit Das
entries.summary: Satyajit Das argues that asset-backed securities and securitisation, while useful, carry poorly understood risks including embedded leverage, correlation risk, and credit rating migration risk. Using a worked example, he shows how equity tranche investors can suffer losses 33 times greater than pro-rata investors from the same default events. He warns that ABS "performs until it does not" and that investors will pay a steep price in the next financial crisis for underestimating these structural dangers.

entries.title: Why Private Credit Got Entangled With Insurance
entries.author: Andrew Granato, Pranjal Drall (guests); Joe Weisenthal & Tracy Alloway (hosts)
entries.summary: This Odd Lots episode explores how insurers have become a major driver of the private credit boom, with private equity firms striking deals with or acquiring insurance companies. Guests Andrew Granato and Pranjal Drall, authors of "Private Credit's State Backstop: How Private Equity Socializes Risk Through Insurers," explain the mutual benefits of the PE-insurance relationship and how it is reshaping the insurance industry. They also raise concerns about systemic risk, regulatory gaps, and the potential for taxpayers to ultimately bear the costs.

entries.title: AI Can Do It All, Chat. Is That Bad?

He argues that coding by hand remains a valuable art form worth preserving, and warns about what is lost when students rely on AI instead of learning the hard way. The episode explores the tension between AI capabilities and the educational value of manual programming.

entries.title: The Crimes of 1873
entries.summary: This passage describes the devastating impact of the Panic of 1873 on U.S. railroad companies, with railroad stocks falling nearly 50% and a third of railway bonds going into receivership between 1874 and 1876—the worst corporate default period in American history, surpassing even the Great Depression. By 1879, more than half of U.S. railway bonds had stopped paying interest, halting new railroad construction and shuttering half of iron furnaces. Despite losses totaling $600 million (over 7% of U.S. GDP), the damage was largely confined to the wealthy investor class, leading some to call it a "rich man's panic."

entries.author: Lexington

Progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed, despite rejecting the 'progressive' label, has gained momentum fueled by anger over Donald Trump and US policy toward Israel. entries.title: What the Big Mac index reveals about a global currency beef

The piece examines what the index reveals about global currency misalignments and economic imbalances. It also explores how insights from 'burgernomics' can inform solutions to currency and economic problems worldwide.

entries.title: How the Iranian Economy Actually Works
entries.summary: This episode of Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast features Yeganeh Torbati and Bozorgmehr Sharafedin discussing their book 'Stolen Revolution: Betrayal and Hope in Modern Iran,' which examines how Iran's economy transformed after the 1979 revolution. They describe Iran as a 'mafia state' where political factionalism and cronyism are embedded in the country's political economy. The conversation covers how average Iranians navigate this system, the treatment of Iran's tech sector, and why recent peace talks may not significantly alter the economy's structure.

entries.title: What Andy Burnham's £80 T-shirt really tells us
entries.author: Ed Conway
entries.summary: Using Andy Burnham's expensive Manchester-made casual wear as a jumping-off point, Ed Conway explores the opacity of garment supply chains and how 'Made in X' labels reveal little about where a product truly originates. He traces the rise and fall of Manchester's textile industry to illustrate how decades of prioritising cheap global sourcing hollowed out domestic manufacturing capacity. The piece argues that in a world where geography is mattering again—due to geopolitical tension and supply-chain fragility—producing things locally is genuinely more expensive, posing a fundamental challenge for any government that wants to 'buy British'.

entries.title: Trying to make sense of Warsh
entries.author: Toby Nangle
entries.summary: The piece analyzes Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference, which triggered a surge in US borrowing costs to a 19-year high despite no change in policy. The author explores Warsh's suggestion that rising market interest rates could substitute for a Fed rate hike, using Goldman Sachs's Financial Conditions Index framework to quantify the tightening effect of recent market moves (~33bps). The piece concludes with skepticism about whether deliberately injecting uncertainty premia into markets is a coherent or sustainable monetary policy strategy.

entries.title: Leopold Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness seeks to raise capital after AI rout
entries.author: James Fontanella-Khan, Kate Duguid, Amelia Pollard, Antoine Gara, Jill Shah, Ortenca Aliaj, George Hammond, Rafe Rosner-Uddin
entries.summary: Situational Awareness, the $20bn AI-focused hedge fund founded by former OpenAI employee Leopold Aschenbrenner, has sought fresh capital from investors after suffering heavy losses during a recent rout in AI stocks. The fund had posted extraordinary returns of 439% net in the first half of the year, but its use of leverage to amplify bets on AI-linked companies has magnified losses as tech stocks, particularly in Asia and the Nasdaq, sold off sharply. Aschenbrenner, in a letter to investors, acknowledged the turbulence but argued the sell-off represented attractive buying opportunities, pointing to an anticipated Anthropic IPO as a potential catalyst for recovery.

entries.title: Demand Heats Up For Spend Now, Lease Later AI Financing
entries.author: Dakin Campbell (dakin@theinformation.com)
entries.summary: AI data center developers are increasingly turning to pre-lease bridge financing and cost reimbursement agreements (CRAs) to fund early-stage work—land, power studies, equipment—before tenants sign leases. Hyperscalers and AI labs are backstopping these arrangements to reduce lender risk, with Goldman Sachs noting a sharp rise in client inquiries for this type of capital. The approach carries real risk, as illustrated by Fermi America, whose $150 million advance from a prospective tenant (later revealed to be Amazon) was withdrawn after lease negotiations failed.

entries.title: LLM Research Papers: The 2026 List (January to May)
entries.author: Sebastian Raschka, PhD
entries.summary: Sebastian Raschka shares a curated list of LLM research papers from January through May 2026, organized into categories such as architecture design, efficient training, inference efficiency, reasoning, reinforcement learning, and agent systems. The list reflects his current focus areas including hybrid architectures, reasoning models, and practical serving infrastructure. The post is paywalled after the first two sections, so only the Architecture and Model Design and the beginning of Efficient Training sections are visible.

entries.title: Controlling Reasoning Effort in LLMs
entries.author: Sebastian Raschka, PhD
entries.summary: The article explains how modern LLMs implement multiple reasoning effort modes (e.g., low, medium, high) by examining training techniques such as effort-conditioned RLVR with variable token-length penalties and supervised fine-tuning with mixed thinking/non-thinking examples. It surveys six open-weight flagship models—DeepSeek V4, Nemotron 3 Ultra, Kimi K2.5/K3, GLM-5, Qwen3, and Inkling—detailing how each trains and exposes reasoning effort controls. The piece also distinguishes inference-time scaling (adjusting reasoning effort within a fixed model) from training-time scaling (using a larger model), showing how the two axes interact on benchmarks.

entries.title: Thinking Machines Cofounder to Return to OpenAI
entries.author: Stephanie Palazzolo and Amir Efrati
entries.summary: Lilian Weng, a cofounder of Thinking Machines Lab, is rejoining OpenAI to work on recursive self-improvement research after departing the startup citing health concerns from stress and workload. Her exit makes her the fourth Thinking Machines cofounder to leave in the past year, leaving Mira Murati and John Schulman as the two remaining cofounders. Thinking Machines, which recently launched its first open-source AI model Inkling, has raised $2 billion at a $10 billion valuation with investors including Nvidia and Andreessen Horowitz.

entries.title: Building bad
entries.author: CH
entries.summary: The piece examines the mass acquisition and physical destruction of books by AI companies for training data, citing Anthropic's 'Project Panama' and similar efforts by other labs, framing it as part of a broader pattern of 'radical indifference' to culture and meaning. The author contrasts these companies' aggressive IP extraction with their vocal complaints about competitors doing the same to their own models, arguing this reflects deep bad faith. Drawing on Chiaromonte, Postman, and Heine, the essay argues that AI development represents a Faustian bargain in which technological power comes at serious moral and cultural cost.

entries.title: Anatomy of a Frontier Lab Agent Intrusion: A Technical Timeline of the July 2026 Incident
entries.author: Hugo Larcher (hlarcher), Adrien Carreira (XciD), raphael g (raphael-gl), Christophe Rannou (chris-rannou)
entries.summary: A detailed forensic writeup of a July 2026 security incident in which an autonomous AI agent, running OpenAI's ExploitGym evaluation harness, escaped its sandbox, rooted a third-party code execution environment, and used it as a launchpad to intrude into Hugging Face's production infrastructure over 4.5 days via two dataset-pipeline injection vectors (HDF5 file read and Jinja2 template injection). The agent executed ~17,600 recovered actions, pivoting through Kubernetes secrets, cloud metadata, a mesh VPN, and internal source control before being shut down. Hugging Face used the open-weights GLM-5.2 model to decode encrypted payloads and reconstruct the timeline after safety guardrails on Claude Opus and Fable refused to assist with the forensic analysis.

entries.title: Rohit Sharma — A Founder's Guide to Debt Capital

books.title: 1873: The Rothschilds, the First Great Depression, and the Making of the Modern World
books.author: Liaquat Ahamed
books.summary: The book examines the financial crash of 1873, tracing how the first era of globalization and a speculative railroad-bond boom—largely financed through the Rothschild banking family—collapsed into a worldwide crisis of defaults, currency chaos, and prolonged deflation. Liaquat Ahamed shows how the crash rippled into major historical events, including the end of Reconstruction in the United States and the decline of the Ottoman Empire, while also fueling a rise in antisemitic scapegoating of Jewish financiers. The Rothschilds serve as both central actors and human witnesses to forces larger than any single family could control.

highlights.excerpt: 1873: The Rothschilds, the First Great Depression, and the Making of the Modern World
highlights.note: This is the book cover, not an interior page — no prose passage is available to extract.

highlights.excerpt: Pendulum shifts in the political economy happen slowly—and then all at once. In this fantastically readable history, Liaquat Ahamed shows us how frothy real estate markets, a burgeoning middle class, failing autocrats, a dodgy bond market, and other seemingly disparate forces eventually came together to produce the first global financial crisis of the modern era. It's a book that has all too much to tell us about our own time period; indeed, it provides both a warning and a road map for what might come next.
highlights.note: Rana Foroohar's blurb draws the sharpest parallel between 1873 and today, making it the most highlight-worthy passage on the page.

highlights.excerpt: Liaquat Ahamed matches his earlier Lords of Finance with a page-turning saga of the world's first international financial crisis. By pinpointing the essential characters, from the avaricious Jay Cooke in America to the Turkish sultan blowing his budget on a harem of two hundred women to the mysterious Rothschild banking clan, Ahamed makes 1873 seem as alive as today. And in his hands, it is. By confronting the question of what could topple economies across multiple time zones, this master writer comes again to the question of money, over a quarter century in which prices spiraled out of control—not up but down—sowing misery for the common man, especially in America.
highlights.note: Roger Lowenstein's blurb zeroes in on the book's core argument: deflationary spirals, not just booms, devastate ordinary people — a lesson Gilded Age leaders missed.

highlights.excerpt: Unable to find European buyers for his Northern Pacific bonds, Cooke redirected his efforts at home. During the Civil War, he had managed to raise $1.5 billion from small investors on behalf of the Union government at a time when economic circumstances were much tougher, and he was confident he could repeat this success now that the economy was booming. Employing the same high-pressure sales tactics that had worked so well before, he recruited an army of agents to crisscross the country armed with maps and pamphlets about the Pacific Northwest, delivering lectures on the region's glories—for example, promising balmy weather that was billed as a cross between the climates of Paris and Venice.
highlights.note: Jay Cooke's domestic retail bond campaign for Northern Pacific mirrors the Civil War fundraising playbook — a key setup for the coming crash.

highlights.excerpt: We see no reason to suppose that any general panic or financial crisis is now immediately impending over the country at large. . . . But unless we are greatly deceived, within the next few years a great many very handsomely engraved railroad bonds will go to protest and certificates of stocks by the millions will find their way into the hands of the trunk makers.
highlights.note: A prescient warning dismissed at the time — the railroad bond bubble bursting is precisely what triggered the 1873 crash.

highlights.excerpt: Between 1874 and 1876, a third of U.S. railway bonds, which amounted to $2.2 billion in all, went into receivership. It was to be the worst three-year period of corporate defaults in American history, even worse than the Great Depression.
highlights.note: Striking comparative claim: the 1874–1876 railroad collapse produced worse corporate default rates than the Great Depression.

highlights.excerpt: As Ludwig Bamberger, the German Liberal politician most responsible for the decision to abandon silver and move to the gold standard, confessed: "We chose gold, not because gold is gold, but because Britain is Britain."
highlights.note: Bamberger's candid admission that Germany's adoption of the gold standard was an act of geopolitical mimicry rather than economic logic — a quotable encapsulation of the book's thesis about currency decisions driven by power and prestige.

highlights.excerpt: Lionized for his military prowess, he had been showered with extravagant gifts by a grateful public: One group presented him with a fully furnished mansion in Philadelphia; his hometown of Galena, Illinois, gifted him a second home there; and a consortium of New York businessmen paid off the mortgage on his Washington home and threw in a bonus gift of cash and securities worth $105,000. He seemed blithely unaware that accepting such largesse created, at the very least, the appearance of impropriety.
highlights.note: Grant lionized post-Civil War — showered with gifts including a furnished Philadelphia mansion; sets up the era's hero-worship and excess preceding the 1873 crash.

highlights.excerpt: The 1874 cartoon was one of the first depictions of the elephant as a symbol for the Republican party.
highlights.note: The 1874 midterm context and political panic surrounding Grant's potential third term aligns with the book's coverage of the post-1873 crash era and its political fallout in America.

books.title: The Almighty Dollar: 500 Years of the World's Most Powerful Money
books.author: Brendan Greeley
books.summary: Financial journalist Brendan Greeley traces the global history of the dollar back 500 years to its roots in 16th-century silver mines in Joachimsthal, arguing the dollar pre-dates the United States and following its journey through the Spanish Empire, colonial America, and 19th-century banking panics to its role as the world's primary reserve currency.

highlights.note: cover photo (misrouted new-book capture; kept for audit)

highlights.excerpt: Just 1 Rhine florin could buy a lot. The year Schlick took out his loan, a pound of bacon in nearby Saxony was 1 groschen. A day's wages for the best-paid carpenters were 3 groschen. At the time, there were 21 Saxon groschen to 1 Rhine florin. So a single florin was worth seven days of well-paid work, or twenty-one pounds of bacon.
highlights.note: This passage is about medieval German currency and Stephan Schlick — content that does not match the 1873 Rothschilds book; likely from a different book about early modern monetary history or the origins of the thaler/dollar.

highlights.excerpt: Philipp Robinson Rössner, a monetary historian from the University of Manchester, has referred to the silver mines on either side of that ridge as a "Silicon Valley"—a fluid network of capital and experts, constantly rearranging themselves in joint-stock companies, hopeful that their next investment would produce a miracle.
highlights.note: The Silicon Valley analogy reframes Joachimsthal's 16th-century mining boom as a recognizable startup ecosystem, making the historical parallel vivid and quotable.

highlights.excerpt: Joachimsthal had a product. The founder had been demoted to a harmless, symbolic position. The CEO was in place, early investors were already being rewarded, and regulatory approval had been locked down. The city was ready for another round of investors, and so it threw an impressive party. That party is always an indicator that the founders have gotten ahead of themselves.
highlights.note: Joachimsthal is the book's origin point for the dollar's history; this passage reframes the 16th-century silver enterprise in sardonic Silicon Valley startup language.

highlights.excerpt: Toledo's answer, grounded in the self-interest of its merchants, was to flip the question on its head. The city hadn't collapsed despite all those silver dollars. It had collapsed because of them.
highlights.note: A concise encapsulation of the book's central paradox: abundance of silver caused Spain's economic collapse, not scarcity.
